title: Food and eating
intro: The most useful concrete nouns in the language, because you will use them every day and can point at them while you learn. Watch the genders: most are predictable from the ending, and the two that are not are flagged.

entries.note: In Mexico la comida on its own usually means the main midday meal.

ex.es: La comida de este país me encanta.
ex.en: I love this country's food.

ex.es: Es la mejor comida que he probado.
ex.en: It's the best meal I've ever tasted.

ex.es: La comida es a las dos.
ex.en: Lunch is at two.

entries.note: The verb is desayunar — one word where English needs three.

ex.en: I have bread and cheese for breakfast.

entries.note: Verb: almorzar (yo almuerzo). Competes regionally with la comida.

ex.en: Shall we have lunch together on Friday?

entries.note: Verb: cenar. Eaten late — nine or ten at night is normal.

ex.en: We eat dinner late on Saturdays.

entries.note: Feminine, but takes el in the singular because agua starts with a stressed a. So el agua fría, and las aguas in the plural.

ex.es: ¿Me trae un vaso de agua, por favor?
ex.en: Could you bring me a glass of water, please?
I buy fresh bread every morning.

entries.note: On a menu carne usually means beef specifically; carne de cerdo is pork.

ex.es: No come carne desde hace años.
ex.en: She hasn't eaten meat for years.
I ordered beef with potatoes.
The roast chicken is delicious.

entries.note: A fish still swimming is el pez. Once it is caught it becomes el pescado — literally the fished.

ex.es: En la costa el pescado es más barato.
ex.en: On the coast fish is cheaper.
How would you like your eggs?
We're out of milk.
Put more cheese on it, please.

entries.note: Uncountable like the English, so la fruta covers the whole category.

ex.es: Come fruta en vez de dulces.
ex.en: Eat fruit instead of sweets.

entries.note: Usually plural: las verduras. la legumbre is a pulse, not a vegetable.

ex.es: Las verduras están en la bolsa verde.
ex.en: The vegetables are in the green bag.
They serve rice with almost everything.

entries.note: Mexico and Central America say frijoles; the Caribbean habichuelas; Spain and the Southern Cone judías or porotos.

ex.es: Los frijoles negros son mis favoritos.
ex.en: Black beans are my favourite.

entries.note: Feminine despite ending in a consonant. salado means salty.

ex.en: It needs salt.

entries.note: Takes either gender in practice — el azúcar and la azúcar are both heard — but el is safer.

ex.en: I drink my coffee without sugar.

entries.note: About food it means tasty, and it is the everyday compliment to a cook — far commoner than delicioso.

ex.en: The cake is so good!
He's from a wealthy family.

entries.note: La cuenta, por favor is how you end a meal. Waving for the bill is normal.

ex.en: Could you bring us the bill?

ex.es: Abrí una cuenta en ese banco.
ex.en: I opened an account at that bank.

entries.warn: In Argentina, Uruguay, Chile and Paraguay this is a coarse word for the female genitals, and one of the strongest insults in the language. Perfectly ordinary in Mexico, where it names a pastry. Say caracol or caparazón for a shell if you are anywhere near the Southern Cone.

ex.es: Encontramos una concha en la playa.
ex.en: We found a shell on the beach.

ex.es: Dos conchas y un café con leche.
ex.en: Two conchas and a latte.
